body:
I. Under the Chuppah

Before entering the parsha, I want to share a beautiful experience from last night. I was able to be mesameach chassan v'kallah for a family I have known for many years, celebrating the marriage of their youngest daughter. There is something amazing about standing under a chuppah, watching two people come together, choosing to build a new life with Torah, with Hashem, and with one another. And what a week to get married, the week of Parshas Bereishis. Because they are not simply entering a partnership with each other. They are entering a partnership with Hashem.

That is not a homiletic flourish. It is something we find explicitly in the parsha. When Kayin is born, the Torah records Chava's words:

קניתי איש את ה׳

"I have acquired a man together with Hashem."

— Bereishis 4:1

Rashi explains the phrase beautifully: כשברא אותי ואת אישי הוא לבדו בראנו אבל בזה שותפים אנו עמו. When Hashem created Adam and Chava, He alone created them, but in bringing this child into the world, they became partners with Him. The word Rashi uses is shutafim, partners. That is exactly what a chassan and kallah are beginning under the chuppah. A partnership that can bring new life into the world, in which they are never working only with each other, but always with Hashem as the third partner.

II. Creation and Partnership

We begin the Torah again with Hashem creating the world. Six days of creation, and on the seventh, Shabbos. We know the account well. We recite Vayechulu every Friday night. But there is always more to understand. When Hashem comes to the creation of Adam, He says something striking:

נעשה אדם בצלמנו כדמותנו

"Let us make man in our image, after our likeness."

— Bereishis 1:26

Why does Hashem speak in the plural? Rashi explains that Hashem was consulting His heavenly court, teaching us שיהא הגדול נמלך ונוטל רשות מן הקטן, that the greater should consult and seek permission from the lesser. Hashem did not need the malachim in order to create Adam. And yet He modeled, at the very moment before creating the first human being, a lesson in humility. Even when one side is greater, more capable, more knowledgeable, that does not erase the value of involving another. Before the first partnership between people even existed, Hashem was already showing us what partnership looks like.

We are created b'tzelem Elokim, but that clearly does not mean we are physically like Hashem or that we share His limitless abilities. Rashi explains כדמותנו as להבין ולהשכיל, the capacity to understand and discern. And what was Hashem doing throughout creation? Bringing the world into existence, establishing order, giving life, providing for His creations. We can see creation through the attributes of chesed and gevurah. Hashem gives and gives, but He also creates distinctions and boundaries. Day and night. Heaven and earth. Land and sea. And then humanity receives an extraordinary responsibility, פרו ורבו, be fruitful and multiply, and Adam is placed in Gan Eden לעבדה ולשמרה, to work it and to guard it. He is given a real role within creation itself.

And there is a detail in the Rashi on Chava's words that is easy to miss. Rashi explains that the birth of Kayin took place before the sin of the Eitz HaDaas, even though it is recorded afterward. The partnership of husband, wife, and Hashem was already woven into the world before anything went wrong. It was not something humanity developed as a response to its failure. It was there from the start. Hashem does not need our help. He could bring every soul into the world entirely on His own. And still He gives us the opportunity to participate.

III. What Fruits Are We Producing?

On the simplest level, פרו ורבו is the mitzvah of having children. A mother, a father, Hashem, and then, be'ezras Hashem, children. But I want to take this idea of fruitfulness and hold it up as a broader way of thinking about our whole participation in creation. We have pri ha'eitz and pri ha'adamah, the fruits of the tree and of the ground, and we make a brachah on them. But we also speak about the fruits of our labor, the things we plant in the world that are not literal fruit at all.

When I teach my children a word of Torah, I am planting something. When I smile at someone, help another person, set an example, say the right word at the right moment, I may be setting something into motion that continues far beyond me. Machshavah, dibur, and ma'aseh. Thought, speech, and action. Hashem created the world through speech, and while we certainly cannot create yesh me'ayin, something out of absolute nothingness, the way He does, we can use the abilities He gave us to shape the world around us. Our words can build. Our actions can cultivate. Our thoughts can become the beginning of something greater.

And this leads to a question that sits underneath the whole parsha. We are told to be fruitful and to multiply, to increase, to make greater. There is a beautiful resonance between the pri we are meant to produce and the ribui, the increase, we are meant to bring about. But the question is always: what am I making greater, and for whom? Am I growing simply for myself, or am I growing so that I will have more to give?

IV. Two Kings and One Crown

There is an illustration of this question hidden in creation itself, before Adam is even formed. The Torah first describes two great luminaries and then, in the same breath, distinguishes between the greater luminary and the lesser one. Chazal explain that the two were originally created equal, and the moon was diminished after it objected:

אי אפשר לשני מלכים שישתמשו בכתר אחד

"Two kings cannot make use of one crown."

— Chullin 60b

I do not want to flatten that entire sugya into a simple story about arrogance, because the Gemara has a far richer discussion, and Hashem ultimately gives the moon great consolation. But for our purposes, there is something worth sitting with in the question itself. Why do we so often assume that another person's greatness diminishes our own? Why must growth become a competition? And especially within a partnership, why should one person's accomplishments ever come at the expense of the other? That question takes us straight into the moral choices that follow.

V. The Danger of Wanting More

Adam receives one command concerning the Eitz HaDaas Tov VaRa. He may eat from every other tree of the Gan, but not from this one. When Chava later speaks with the nachash, she adds something to the command, saying ולא תגעו בו, that they may not even touch it. Rashi explains הוסיפה על הציווי לפיכך באה לידי גרעון, that she added to the command, and precisely that addition became a source of failure. The nachash pushed her against the tree and said: just as touching it did not kill you, eating from it will not kill you either.

There is a lesson in that for us. Not every increase is an improvement. Even when we are trying to add, to build a fence, to make something greater, we have to keep returning to what Hashem actually asked of us. And perhaps there is another dimension in the very name of the tree, the knowledge of tov and ra. I am not suggesting for a moment that the Torah discourages knowledge or growth; the opposite is true, since the Torah demands that we learn and develop our daas. But the episode invites us to feel the difference between growth that follows Hashem's instruction and growth we pursue simply because something looks desirable. Adam and Chava were given abundance, with one single boundary, and they crossed it. As Rabbi Gerzi calls it, the tree-eating boo-boo experience. And immediately, instead of taking responsibility, they begin shifting blame. The relationship between them changes, the relationship between humanity and Hashem changes, and the consequences reach through all the generations that follow.

VI. Giving or Keeping

Then we come to Kayin and Hevel. Two brothers, two occupations. Kayin works the ground, Hevel tends the flock. Both produce something from the world Hashem gave them, and both bring a korban. It is worth noticing that Kayin is actually the first to bring an offering at all. The contrast the Torah draws is not between a brother who gives and a brother who does not. Both give. The difference is in what they choose to give.

Of Kayin the Torah says simply ויבא קין מפרי האדמה מנחה לה׳, that he brought an offering from the fruit of the ground. But of Hevel it says והבל הביא גם הוא מבכרות צאנו ומחלבהן, from the firstborn of his flock and from the choicest portions. Rashi understands Kayin's offering as having come from inferior produce. The Torah itself emphasizes the quality of what Hevel brought.

Now the Torah does not tell us outright what Kayin was thinking. It does not quote him saying, "I will keep the best for myself." That is an interpretation of his priorities, not a transcript of his thoughts. But the contrast in the offerings lets us ask a fair question. Perhaps Hevel was thinking: Hashem has given me so much, I get to keep so much, and I want to give something beautiful back to Him. And perhaps Kayin was thinking: why should I give Him my finest when I can keep that for myself and give Him something lesser? When Hashem gives me an entire world to benefit from, am I asking what I can give back, or am I calculating the least I can give while holding onto the most? That is the real question of fruitfulness. It is not how much I produce. It is what I choose to do with the fruits of my labor.

And then Kayin becomes jealous, because his brother's offering was accepted and his own was not. But Hashem does not abandon him. He tells him ואתה תמשל בו, that he can rule over it, and Rashi explains אם תרצה תתגבר עליו, if you want, you can overcome it. This is extraordinary. Kayin has already made a poor choice, and yet he is not trapped by it. He has bechirah. He can still respond differently, still choose tov. Tragically, he does not, and he kills his brother. The same world in which humanity was given the power to cultivate and create becomes a world in which humanity uses that very power to destroy. That is the weight that comes with being a partner.

VII. Humanity Continues Forward

It is easy to look at these opening generations and see only their failures. But the story does not end there. New generations are born, and people keep building the world. We reach Mesushelach, whose remarkably long life the Torah records, and Chazal describe him as a tzaddik. Rashi, on the seven days before the Mabul, explains that those days corresponded to the mourning for Mesushelach HaTzaddik, and that Hashem delayed the punishment out of regard for his honor. Mesushelach was the father of Lemech, and Lemech the father of Noach, and our parsha ends with ונח מצא חן בעיני ה׳, that Noach found favor in Hashem's eyes. Even as humanity declined, there remained individuals whose lives could be turned toward something different. The opportunity to serve Hashem was never gone. The ability to choose good was never gone.

VIII. Returning to the Chuppah

Which brings me back to that chuppah from last night, because a marriage can illustrate all of this in a very practical way. I have seen situations where a person wants to become greater because of who their spouse is. They want status, recognition, a feeling of importance, and the spouse becomes a means of elevating themselves. That is not the partnership we have been describing. A genuine partnership is the opposite. It is when I want to become a greater person for my spouse, when I want to grow because I want to give more, contribute more, and build something together with the other person rather than at their expense.

My wife and I are very different people, with different strengths and different approaches, and we do not need to be identical. After all, I was created b'tzelem Elokim, and I am certainly not capable of what Hashem is capable of. Partnership never required equality of abilities. It requires a shared purpose. We can approach things in completely different ways and still want to bring the same kinds of goodness into the world. Our pri, the fruits of our partnership, include our children, but also our teaching, our learning, and the influence we have on the people around us. We do not have to produce those fruits in the same way. We only have to be working toward the same goal. And when we bring Hashem into that partnership, we are returning to the very purpose of creation: to cultivate rather than destroy, to give rather than simply take, to support rather than compete, and to use our bechirah to bring more tov into the world.

IX. An Opportunity to Begin Again

And perhaps that is one of the most beautiful messages of Bereishis. We are starting the Torah again. We have come through Tishrei, through Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkos, and Simchas Torah, and now we begin again from the very beginning. We get to look at the world with fresh eyes and ask the oldest questions as if for the first time. Why am I here? What am I producing? What am I making greater? What am I choosing to give?

Even Adam's own story holds that message of a second chance. Hashem had warned him כי ביום אכלך ממנו מות תמות, that on the day he ate from the tree he would surely die, and yet the Torah records that Adam went on to live nine hundred and thirty years. This is not Hashem arguing His way out of the decree. It is a question of whose day we are counting. Chazal reconcile the timeline through the pasuk in Tehillim, כי אלף שנים בעיניך כיום אתמול, that a thousand years in Hashem's eyes are like a single passing day. Measured by Hashem's own day, Adam did die within the very day he ate, falling short of completing that thousand-year day by exactly seventy years. The point is not that the sin carried no consequence, because it certainly did. The point is that Adam was given the opportunity to go on living, building, and bringing generations into the world. That too is part of our partnership. We are imperfect, and we are given the ability to choose what we do next, to make the next action better, the next words more meaningful, and the next fruits of our labor something we can give back to Hashem and to the world.

What a beautiful way to enter Shabbos Bereishis. May we have a year of meaningful growth, of strong partnerships, of giving and building, and of using the opportunities Hashem gives us to bring more tov into His world.

חזק ואחזק

Good Shabbos, Good Chodesh, and a Shana Tova.

Reflection Questions

• When I think about growth and increase in my own life, what am I actually making greater, and for whom am I making it greater?

• Am I growing simply to have more for myself, or am I growing so that I will have more to give back to Hashem and to others?

• Like Kayin and Hevel, I give to Hashem in many ways. Am I offering Him my firstborn and my finest, or quietly keeping the best for myself?

• Where in my life am I adding fences and stringencies that go beyond what Hashem actually asked, the way Chava added to the command, and is that addition truly serving me?

• In my closest partnerships, am I trying to become greater because of the other person, or am I trying to become greater for the other person?

• Bereishis offers a fresh beginning. What is one fruit, in thought, speech, or action, that I want to plant into the world this year?
